title: Euclid's lemma: a prime dividing a product divides a factor
statement: If p is prime and p divides a*b, then p divides a or p divides b. Here `p is prime` means 2 <= p and every divisor of p is 1 or p.

formal.statement: theorem Nat.euclid_lemma : ((p : AxNat) -> ((a : AxNat) -> ((b : AxNat) -> ((hp : (And (AxNat.le (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) p) ((d : AxNat) -> ((hd : AxNat.dvd d p) -> Or (Eq.{1} AxNat d (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) (Eq.{1} AxNat d p))))) -> ((h : AxNat.dvd p (AxNat.mul a b)) -> Or (AxNat.dvd p a) (AxNat.dvd p b))))))

provenance.source: proposition extracted from the S:number strand of the math-education concept graph; statement authored here, nothing copied

prior_art.attribution: standard textbook attribution; this lane did not consult the primary source

notes: Stated INSTEAD of unique factorisation itself, which is the concept it came from: the kernel has no list, multiset or finite-product vocabulary, so `n is a product of primes, unique up to order` cannot be written in its language at all today. Euclid's lemma is the mathematical content of the uniqueness half and IS expressible. Reachable from the stated dependencies: gcd(p, a) divides p, so it is 1 or p, and the Bezout certificate turns the first case into p | b. formal.statement is written in the SAME core rendering the kernel emits for its own theorems, and uses ONLY symbols `build_nat_prelude` actually declares (checked against the 119-theorem inventory dumped on 2026-08-14), so it can be dispatched without inventing vocabulary. Primality is spelled out inline because the prelude has no `Prime` predicate. Binders carry readable names rather than the kernel's `x0, x1, ...`; that is a pretty-printing difference only, and any admitted proof would render with positional names.
